collection: NERDC JSS 1 Mathematics directed numbers and fraction operations
note: Original classroom practice. Independent academic review pending.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Subtract a whole number by regrouping through consecutive zero places.
questions.prompt: A water tank meter showed 6,002 L at the start of a filling period and 9,000 L at the end. How many litres were added?
questions.explanation: The reading rose by 2,998 L: adding 2,998 to 6,002 gives 9,000.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Explain the place value of a digit created by regrouping in a sum.
questions.prompt: Two carton counts, 5,680 and 2,740, are added. In the total, what is the value of the digit in the thousands place? Explain how the hundreds contribute to this digit.
questions.answer: 8,000. The 6 hundreds and 7 hundreds make 13 hundreds. The tens also carry 1 hundred, so the hundreds column gives 14 hundreds, which carries 1 thousand.
questions.explanation: The tens give 12 tens, so 1 hundred carries. Then 14 hundreds regroup as 1 thousand and 4 hundreds. The thousands are 5 + 2 + 1 = 8.

markingGuide.description: Gives the place value as 8,000.
Identifies the hundred carried from the tens column.
Explains the thousand carried from the hundreds column.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.subtopic: Coordinates relative to a reference point
questions.learningObjective: Represent directed positions on a number line with a defined origin.
questions.prompt: On a straight path, a gate is the zero point and east is positive. A bench is 3 m west of the gate and a sign is 4 m east. Draw a number line marking the gate, bench and sign. Label the coordinates of all three.
questions.answer: With east to the right, the bench is at −3, the gate at 0 and the sign at +4.
questions.explanation: West is the negative direction, so the bench is left of zero. East is positive, so the sign is right of zero.

markingGuide.description: Draws a number line with equally spaced unit marks and the gate at 0.
Marks the bench at −3.
Marks the sign at +4.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.subtopic: Subtracting a negative on a line
questions.learningObjective: Explain the direction of a move when subtracting a negative integer.
questions.prompt: A pupil marks −5 on a number line. To show −5 − (−4), the pupil moves four units left. Correct the move and name the end point.
questions.answer: Move four units right from −5 to −1.
questions.explanation: Subtracting −4 undoes a move four units left. The inverse move is four units right.

markingGuide.description: Specifies a four-unit move to the right from −5.
Gives −1 as the end point.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the difference between signed temperatures.
questions.prompt: Two model cold-room displays read −7°C and +2°C. By how many degrees is the second display warmer than the first?
questions.explanation: The rise from −7°C to 0°C is 7 degrees. There are 2 more degrees to +2°C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish net change from final balance in a sequence of transactions.
questions.prompt: A school club cash box starts with ₦2,350. It pays ₦840 for materials, receives ₦510 in dues, and pays ₦275 for transport. Write the net change as a signed amount and give the final balance.
questions.explanation: The transactions sum to −840 + 510 − 275 = −605. The starting balance then falls by ₦605.

markingGuide.description: Assigns a negative sign to payments and a positive sign to dues.
Gives the net change as −₦605.
Gives the final balance as ₦1,745.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Subtract mixed numbers by exchanging one whole for fractional parts.
questions.prompt: Work out 4 1/6 − 2 5/6. Show how to regroup the first mixed number so that you can subtract sixths.
questions.explanation: Exchange one whole for 6/6. Then 3 − 2 = 1 and 7/6 − 5/6 = 2/6 = 1/3.

markingGuide.description: Rewrites 4 1/6 as 3 7/6.
Shows subtraction to get 1 2/6.
Simplifies to 1 1/3.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Identify why adding denominators gives an invalid fraction sum.
questions.prompt: A classmate says 1/4 + 1/6 = 2/10. Which explanation correctly identifies and fixes the error?
questions.answer: The pieces are unequal in size. Rewrite as 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12.
questions.explanation: The fractions must count pieces of the same size before their numerators can be added.
options: The pieces are unequal in size. Rewrite as 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12.
The denominators add to 10. Reduce 2/10 to 1/5.
The smaller denominator sets the unit. Add the numerators to get 2/4.
The larger denominator sets the unit. Add the numerators to get 2/6.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Use fraction subtraction to recover a missing change.
questions.prompt: A roll of twine initially had 2 3/8 m on it. A pupil cut off a piece and measured 1 5/12 m still on the roll. What was the length of the piece?
questions.explanation: Use twenty-fourths. The starting length is 57/24 m and the remaining length is 34/24 m. Their difference is 23/24 m.

markingGuide.description: Models the length cut as the original minus the remainder.
Uses equivalent fractions with a common denominator.
Gives 23/24 m.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.subtopic: Combining uses before testing a limit
questions.learningObjective: Add and subtract fractions to decide how much of a resource remains available.
questions.prompt: A school paints 2/9 of one wall yellow and a different 1/4 of the same wall blue. Can it still paint exactly 1/2 of the whole wall green without covering either colour? How much wall would then be unpainted?
questions.answer: Yes. The unpainted fraction after green is 1/36.
questions.explanation: Yellow and blue occupy 8/36 + 9/36 = 17/36. Adding green uses another 18/36. That leaves 1/36.

markingGuide.description: Finds that the first two colours occupy 17/36.
Shows that 1/2 more fits and gives 1/36 unpainted.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Use an equal-cell area model to explain a product of proper fractions.
questions.prompt: Divide a unit square into 5 equal columns and 7 equal rows. Shade the first 3 columns with diagonal strokes and the first 2 rows with horizontal strokes. What fraction has both kinds of shading? Explain the multiplication shown.
questions.explanation: Each cell has area 1/35. The overlap is 3 columns by 2 rows, which is 6 cells.

markingGuide.description: Draws a 5-by-7 grid and indicates the two shaded regions.
Identifies six overlapping cells.
Connects the overlap to 3/5 × 2/7 and gives 6/35.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Predict how dividing a positive quantity by a proper fraction affects the quotient.
questions.prompt: Which expression gives a result larger than 9/10?
questions.explanation: A divisor of 3/5 is smaller than one, so a quantity of 9/10 contains more than 9/10 groups of that size. The quotient is 3/2.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Apply a fractional share to the remaining stock after an initial use.
questions.prompt: A tailor has 18 m of cloth. She uses one third of it for banners, then uses three quarters of the remaining cloth for table covers. How many metres go to the table covers?
questions.explanation: One third of 18 m is 6 m, leaving 12 m. Three quarters of 12 m is 9 m.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a fractional quotient as whole portions and convert the remainder back to the original unit.
questions.prompt: A cook has 5 1/4 L of juice and fills bottles that each hold 2/3 L. How many bottles can be filled completely, and how much juice remains in the jug?
questions.explanation: The quotient is 63/8 = 7 7/8 bottles. Seven full bottles use 14/3 L. Subtracting this amount from 21/4 L leaves 7/12 L.

markingGuide.description: Sets up division by the capacity of one bottle or an equivalent model.
Identifies 7 complete bottles.
Computes 7/12 L remaining.

verification.purpose: Check the quotient in bottle units.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Divide a mixed-number quantity into a specified number of equal shares.
questions.prompt: A weaver divides 3 3/5 m of cord equally among six pupils. A seventh pupil later joins, so they put the cord back together and divide it equally among all seven. How much shorter is each new share than each original share?
questions.explanation: The original share is (18/5) ÷ 6 = 3/5 m. The new share is (18/5) ÷ 7 = 18/35 m. Subtracting gives 21/35 − 18/35 = 3/35 m.

markingGuide.description: Finds the original share of 3/5 m.
Finds the new share of 18/35 m.
Gives a reduction of 3/35 m.
